questions.q: What is the default join type if you omit it from df.join()?
options: "inner" — only rows with matching keys on both sides
"left" — every row from the left DataFrame is always kept
"full" — every row from both DataFrames regardless of match
There is no default; a join type must always be specified
questions.explain: "inner", "left", "right", and "full" are the four core join types.

questions.q: What happens to a row in a left join when its key has no match on the right side?
options: The row is kept, with null values in the columns that came from the right-hand DataFrame
The row is silently dropped from the result entirely
The join raises an error immediately
The row is duplicated once for every row on the right side
questions.explain: This connects straight back to Lesson 51 — checking for these new nulls afterward uses the exact same .isNull() pattern.

questions.q: Why would trips.join(zones, ...) with a left join usually be the right choice for this dataset?
options: You want every trip record kept, even if a PULocationID rarely doesn't match any row in the zone lookup
Left joins are always faster than inner joins regardless of the data
Left joins are required whenever two DataFrames share a column name
Inner joins can never be used with real NYC Taxi data
questions.explain: An inner join would silently drop any trip whose PULocationID has no matching zone.

questions.q: Why does referring to a shared column name by a plain string after a join cause an ambiguous-column error?
options: Because Spark can't tell which of the two DataFrames' matching-named columns you mean
Plain strings are never allowed anywhere after a join
It only happens when using an inner join, never other join types
It's actually never ambiguous — this scenario doesn't occur in PySpark
questions.explain: Referencing the column through its original DataFrame variable, like trips.VendorID vs. zones.VendorID, resolves it.

questions.q: What real-world problem does joining trips with the zone lookup table solve?
options: Trip records only store a numeric PULocationID — the join turns that into an actual readable Zone and Borough
It removes all duplicate trips from the dataset
It converts every column in trips to a different data type
It has no practical purpose beyond combining row counts
questions.explain: This is the real-world payoff of the dataset having a separate zone lookup table at all.
